newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Investment, low liquidity pushes Budapest BUX.
newsitem.headline: Investment, low liquidity pushes Budapest BUX.

text.p: Investment opportunities and low liquidity have made the Budapest bourse (BSE) one of the best performers in the world, ABN AMRO Hoare Govett said on Thursday.

"With yesterday's results, Hungary is again at the top of the list and is the best performing market in 1996," Peter Budahazy, managing director at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett (Hungary) Rt, told a conference on Hungarian capital markets.
The BUX index has risen more than 2,000 points in 1996 reaching its last all-time high on Wednesday when it closed at 3,789.22 points. In dollar terms it has gained more than 100 percent.
"This is the result of both a growing appetite and a shortage of supply in securities," Budahazy said.
The BSE offers investment opportunities in 44 stocks, but many of these issues remain short of foreign investors' size requirements, he said.
"There are so few investment opportunities and so few companies that (are suitable) for these institutional investors."

While the Hungarian market is dominated by dedicated emerging equity market funds, global equity funds also began to build up portfolios on the BSE this year, he said, adding that pension funds, insurance companies and banks are about to enter the market.
The dedicated emerging market funds usually regard $100 million as the lower limit for a company's individual market capitalisation, Budahazy said.
"This ($100 million threshold) is quite tough for Hungarian companies," he said.

Currently only about one-third of the listed firms, including pharmaceuticals companies Richter and Egis, chemicals firms Borsodchem and TVK and oil and gas company MOL, fall into the above-$100 million category.
The Budapest bourse's total equity market capitalisation was 733.08 billion forints at the end of October.
Availability of blocks of shares also causes difficulties and is often time consuming, Budahazy said, adding that funds' usual minimum requirement level for blocks of shares was $250,000.

Unlike on more developed and bigger markets where stock exchange listed companies reflect a country's economic structure, whole sectors are entirely lacking on the six-and-half-year-old Budapest bourse.

"Very often investors like a sector and they would like to invest in one sector," Budahazy said. "There are several sectors which are not represented at all or if they are, (it is) to such a small extent that it is not satisfactory."
"Unfortunately I do not expect a big change...in the coming five to ten years," Budahazy added.
